title: Introduction to ADO.NET and Data Access
description: Understand ADO.NET architecture, connected vs disconnected models, core components, and data providers.

data.text: **ADO.NET** is a set of classes in .NET that allows applications to interact with data sources such as relational databases, XML files, and more. In ASP.NET Core, ADO.NET provides the foundational data access technology for working with databases like Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Oracle.

terms.definition: A data access technology in .NET that enables applications to connect to databases, execute commands, and process results.
A set of classes optimized for communicating with a specific database, such as SqlClient for SQL Server.
An object that represents a session with a SQL Server database.
An object that executes a SQL statement or stored procedure against a database.
A forward-only, read-only stream of data from a database, used in connected mode.
An object that fills a DataTable or DataSet and updates the database, used in disconnected mode.

data.text: ADO.NET supports two primary data access patterns. Choosing the right one depends on your scenario, data volume, and performance requirements.

data.caption: Connected vs Disconnected data access patterns in ADO.NET
data.definition:
graph LR
    A[Application] --> B{Access Pattern}
    B -->|Connected| C[Open SqlConnection]
    B -->|Disconnected| D[SqlDataAdapter Fill]
    C --> E[Create SqlCommand]
    E --> F[ExecuteReader]
    F --> G[Read with SqlDataReader]
    G --> H[Close Connection]
    D --> I[DataTable in Memory]
    I --> J[Work Offline]
    J --> K[Update Database]

data.text: In a **Connected Environment**, the application maintains an open connection to the database for the entire duration of the operation. You typically use **SqlConnection**, **SqlCommand**, and **SqlDataReader** together. This approach is memory-efficient for reading large volumes of data sequentially, but the connection must remain open until processing is complete.

data.title: When to use Connected mode
data.text: Use the connected approach when streaming large result sets row-by-row or when you need the lowest memory footprint. Always close connections as soon as possible using a using statement.

In a **Disconnected Environment**, data is retrieved into an in-memory cache like a **DataTable**, the connection is closed immediately, and you work with the data locally. The **SqlDataAdapter** manages opening and closing the connection automatically. This pattern is ideal when you need to manipulate data without holding a database connection.
ADO.NET is built around several core objects. Each has a specific responsibility in the data access workflow.

rows: Manages the physical connection to the database
Executes SQL statements or stored procedures
Reads data forward-only, read-only in connected mode
Fills DataTable/DataSet and updates the database
Represents a named parameter for parameterized queries

data.text: A **Data Provider** is a set of classes optimized for a specific database. The .NET Framework includes providers for SQL Server, OLE DB, ODBC, and Oracle. Each provider follows the same patterns but uses database-specific class names.

cards.title: SqlClient
cards.description: The .NET Data Provider for SQL Server. Optimized for Microsoft SQL Server and Azure SQL Database.

cards.title: OleDb
cards.description: Provides data access for OLE DB data sources, useful for legacy databases without a native .NET provider.

cards.title: Odbc
cards.description: The ODBC Data Provider for databases that have an ODBC driver but no native .NET provider.

cards.title: OracleClient
cards.description: The .NET Data Provider for Oracle databases.

data.text: For this module, we will focus on the **SqlClient** provider, which is the most commonly used provider in ASP.NET Core applications targeting SQL Server or Azure SQL Database.
Most ADO.NET types live in the **System.Data** namespace and provider-specific sub-namespaces. Here are the key namespaces you will use:

rows: Core ADO.NET types shared by all providers, such as DataTable and DataSet.
The .NET Data Provider for SQL Server, containing SqlConnection, SqlCommand, SqlDataReader, and SqlDataAdapter.
The newer, cross-platform SQL Server provider recommended for .NET Core and .NET 5+.

data.title: Modern .NET note
data.text: In .NET Framework, System.Data.SqlClient was the standard. In .NET Core and .NET 5+, Microsoft.Data.SqlClient is the recommended package. Both work similarly; this module uses SqlClient terminology for clarity.
Where ADO.NET Fits in ASP.NET Core

ADO.NET is the low-level data access layer beneath higher-level ORMs like Entity Framework Core. While EF Core is often preferred for rapid development, understanding ADO.NET helps you diagnose performance issues, write high-performance bulk operations, and use stored procedures efficiently.

items: Diagnose performance issues in data access code
Write high-performance bulk insert and update operations
Execute stored procedures with precise control
Understand what happens behind the scenes of any .NET data access library

data.title: Quick Check
data.description: Test your understanding of ADO.NET basics before moving on.
steps: Name the two data access patterns supported by ADO.NET.
List the three core objects used in connected mode.
Explain the role of SqlDataAdapter in disconnected mode.
data.expectedOutcome: You can clearly explain connected vs disconnected data access and identify the core ADO.NET objects.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: ADO.NET provides connected and disconnected data access patterns.
SqlConnection, SqlCommand, and SqlDataReader are the core objects for connected mode.
SqlDataAdapter and DataTable enable disconnected, in-memory data manipulation.
Data Providers abstract database-specific details behind a common interface.
data.takeaway: You now understand the ADO.NET landscape. In the next lesson, you will set up a real SQL Server database and ASP.NET Core project to start writing data access code.
